opus-5.5.text:
I think the main thing those wide ranges tell you is that people are genuinely very uncertain, and I think that's actually the appropriate state to be in. When you ask someone when a particular milestone will happen, say, when AI will be able to write a bestselling novel or do the job of a surgeon, and the gap between their 25th and 75th percentile is decades, that's not necessarily a sign that they're confused. It may be a fairly honest reflection of how hard this is to forecast.

But there's a second layer, which is that the spread isn't only within individuals; it's also across people. If you look at the aggregate distribution, part of the width comes from different researchers having quite different views. Some people expect things very soon, and some expect them much later, or think they may not happen this century at all. So the aggregate range combines individual uncertainty with real disagreement within the field.

And then there's a third thing I always want to flag, which is that the answers are quite sensitive to how you ask the question. We've found consistently that if you ask people "in what year will there be a 50% chance of this?" versus "what's the probability this happens by a given year?", you get noticeably different answers, with the second framing tending to produce later timelines. Similarly, asking about the automation of all occupations versus the point where AI can do every task better than humans gives answers that are wildly different, even though logically they should be pretty close. So some of the width is people's views being not very stable, and that suggests we shouldn't treat any single number as a precise estimate.

So my overall interpretation is: don't read too much into the median as though it were a confident prediction. The more important takeaway is that a substantial share of AI researchers put meaningful probability on transformative capabilities arriving fairly soon, within a couple of decades or less, while also giving real weight to it taking much longer. If you're making decisions, about policy, safety research, or your own career, I think you should take that whole distribution seriously rather than anchoring on one date. The uncertainty itself is decision-relevant: if there's even, say, a 25% chance of something enormously consequential happening within the next ten or fifteen years, that's worth preparing for.

r001.rationale: The response says the aggregate range combines individual uncertainty with disagreement across forecasters, so its width does not directly represent disagreement alone.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that those wide ranges are, in a sense, the honest part of the data. When you ask hundreds of machine learning researchers when some milestone will be achieved, and the 25th percentile is, say, five years out and the 75th percentile is thirty or forty years out, that's not a measurement error that you'd want to smooth away. That's actually telling you something real, which is that the people who are closest to this technology don't agree with each other, and many of them individually don't feel confident either.

I'd separate two things. One is the spread across respondents, where some people think a milestone is imminent and others think it's generations away. The other is the spread within a single person's distribution, where we ask for the year they think there's a ten percent chance, a fifty percent chance, a ninety percent chance. Both tend to be wide. And I think the second kind is in some ways more informative, because it means even the optimists are saying "I could easily be off by a decade or two."

How do I interpret that? Mostly as: expertise in building these systems does not translate into expertise in forecasting them. People who are very good at making a model work next quarter have no particular training in predicting what the field does over twenty years, and I think the data reflects that. We also see things that should make you skeptical of taking any point estimate too literally. The answers shift quite a lot depending on how you phrase the question, whether you ask about years or probabilities, whether you frame it as "high-level machine intelligence" or as "automating all occupations." If framing effects can move the median by decades, then the wide percentile ranges are, if anything, understating the real uncertainty.

So I wouldn't read the middle of the range as "the answer" and the tails as noise. I'd read the whole thing as a picture of a community that genuinely doesn't know, and I think the right response to that is to take the near end seriously as a live possibility rather than to average it away. If a quarter of the people building this think it could happen within a few years, that's a reason to prepare for that scenario, even if the median is much later.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes spread across respondents from uncertainty within one person, but it does not clearly state that the percentile interval in the averaged forecast does not directly measure disagreement among individual forecasters. It instead links the interval to both kinds of spread.

astra-6.text:
I think the main thing to take away is that there’s a lot of uncertainty. But it matters what those percentiles describe. If they’re the 25th and 75th percentiles across respondents’ forecasts, then the wide range is telling you that different people have quite different expectations. It isn’t directly telling you how uncertain each person is. You could have people who are individually quite confident but disagree strongly with one another.

If those are instead probabilities supplied by an individual forecaster, then the interval represents their own uncertainty about when the milestone will happen. Either way, I’d be reluctant to focus too much on the median date and treat it as a prediction that this is when the thing happens. The range is an important part of the result.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that if the percentiles are across respondents, the wide range indicates that different forecasters have different expectations. That does not communicate that the interval in an averaged forecast fails to directly measure disagreement among individual forecasters.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main thing is that people are very uncertain about when these things will happen. If someone’s 25th-percentile date and their 75th-percentile date are decades apart, they’re putting substantial probability across a very wide range of timelines. So taking their median and saying, “This researcher thinks it will happen in this year,” loses a lot of information.

There’s also a distinction between uncertainty within a person’s forecast and disagreement between people. You could have researchers with similar median dates who are each very uncertain, or researchers who are individually confident but disagree strongly with one another. Those are different situations. Either way, I’d read the forecasts as probability distributions, rather than as a schedule of when particular milestones are going to arrive.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes an individual forecaster’s uncertainty from disagreement between forecasters, but it does not explain that a wide interval in the averaged forecast does not directly measure that disagreement.
